item.title: Cape Muroto and Tokushima's Wild Pacific Coast — Guide
item.description: South of Tokushima city, the prefecture’s coastline turns wild and elemental as it runs down the Pacific shore toward Cape Muroto, the great cape at the tip of the peninsula that divides Tokushima from Kochi’s Muroto. This is a coast of raw geology and open ocean: sheer rocky headlands, wave-cut platforms of uplifted seabed, crashing surf and vast horizons, quite different from the sheltered Seto Inland Sea in the north. The Muroto area is a UNESCO Global Geopark, its dramatic rock formations telling the story of land rising from the sea.

item.title: Cape Muroto: UNESCO Geopark and Wild Coast — Guide
item.description: Cape Muroto, at the eastern tip of Kochi, is a UNESCO Global Geopark where you can see the earth being made: this is a coast of rapidly uplifting land, where rock once formed deep beneath the sea has been thrust up to form dramatic shores of folded strata, wave-cut platforms and jagged formations. A walking trail and boardwalks lead among the rocks and subtropical plants, with information on the remarkable geology, while the warm Pacific offshore is rich with marine life.

item.title: Uradome Coast: Clear Water and Sea Caves of the Geopark — Guide
item.description: The Uradome Coast, just east of the Tottori Sand Dunes, is one of the most beautiful stretches of the Sea of Japan shore and part of the San’in Kaigan UNESCO Global Geopark. Wave and weather have carved the granite into white cliffs, arches, sea caves, sea-stacks and dozens of pine-topped islets standing in water so clear it looks tropical, shading from emerald in the shallows to deep blue. A cliff-top walking trail links a series of viewpoints and small beaches along the shore, and in the warmer months sightseeing boats and sea-kayak tours thread between the rocks and into the caves.

item.title: Izu Peninsula: Hot Springs, Wild Coasts and a UNESCO Geopark — Guide
item.description: The Izu Peninsula juts into the Pacific south of Mount Fuji, formed over millions of years by volcanic islands colliding with Honshu, a geological origin so distinctive that the entire peninsula is designated a UNESCO Global Geopark. Its dramatic coastlines range from the rugged cliffs and sea caves of the west to white-sand beaches in the south, while inland valleys grow Japan’s finest wasabi, and celebrated onsen towns like Atami and Shuzenji have drawn bathers for centuries, all within a couple of hours of Tokyo.

item.title: Oga Peninsula Coastline & Cape Nyudozaki — Akita Guide
item.description: The Oga Peninsula is a globally significant geopark — dramatic sea cliffs expose 50-million-year-old volcanic strata, and the famous Godzilla Rock at Kanpuzaki is a favourite for sunset photography. Cape Nyudozaki, the windswept grassy tip marked by a striped lighthouse and 40th-parallel monuments, is glorious at sunset. The 60 km coastal drive passes sea caves and fishing villages. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Oga, Akita Hours Always open (sunset best) Admission Free Time needed Half day (coastal drive) Best time Summer–autumn; sunset any clear day What to See Godzilla Rock at Kanpuzaki, a sunset icon.

item.title: Shimane Nature Guide: Oki Islands UNESCO Geopark & Dramatic Coastlines
item.description: Shimane’s most dramatic nature lies offshore. The Oki Islands sit 60 kilometers out in the Sea of Japan — remote enough that ancient Japan used them as an island of exile for deposed emperors and unwanted nobles. Today the islands are a UNESCO Global Geopark, recognized for geological formations that tell 600 million years of tectonic history. On the mainland, the Shimane Peninsula’s rocky Sea of Japan coast and the inland Sanbe volcanic highlands round out a nature itinerary that rewards travelers willing to move beyond the main shrine circuit.

item.title: Tottori Nature Guide: Uradome Coast, Mount Daisen & Seasonal Landscapes
item.description: Tottori’s natural variety is compressed into a narrow geography: a coastline of dunes, sea cliffs, and beaches, then an immediate rise to 1,700m mountain peaks. The San’in coast is one of Japan’s most geologically active stretches of shoreline; the inland mountains carry some of the country’s finest beech forest. The prefecture’s low population density means these landscapes see a fraction of the visitors that equivalent sites in Kyushu or Chubu would attract.
